name: Temoaya Otomi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Andrews, Henrietta. 1949. Phonemes and morphophonemes of Temoayan Otomi. International Journal of American Linguistics 15(4): 213-222. DOI 10.1086/464047.
catalog_locator: secs. 1.4.1-1.4.2, pp. 216-217; compound-stress corollary sec. 3.2, p. 220
catalog_quote: 1.4.1. Root-initial juncture /-/ is identifiable phonetically but is correlated with a morphological phenomenon. /-/ marks the initial syllable of a root morpheme when it is preceded in the word by one syllable or more. Phonetically, /-/ is actualized as stress on the syllable which follows. Stress and tone are not conditioned by one another, except for the probable limitation of the rising glide to stressed (i.e. root) syllables (see 1.3.2.). Unstressed syllables occur both with the high and with the low toneme Stressed syllables may occur with each of the three tonemes. ... A light, secondary stress is sometimes heard on the second syllable before and the second syllable after the first root syllable, as in zàphàni ['zàphà″ní] straw. This stress is not strong enough to be confused with the stress which signals a root-initial juncture. The stress which is characteristic of root-initial juncture is strong and occurs nowhere else. In addition to being stressed, the first syllable of the root is pronounced more deliberately than the other syllables of the word, at least in slow speech. ... 1.4.2. Word juncture is marked by a space. When there is no root-initial juncture /-/ present, the word-initial juncture and the root-initial juncture coincide, being identified by the presence of root-initial stress, as described above.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the root (stem); prefix syllables before it and suffix syllables after it are unstressed, so in unprefixed words stress is word-initial. Stress is independent of the three-way tone contrast (high, low, rising), which is itself fullest on root syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 217: 'A light, secondary stress is sometimes heard on the second syllable before and the second syllable after the first root syllable, as in zàphàni straw. This stress is not strong enough to be confused with the stress which signals a root-initial juncture.'
new_statements.exceptions: Tone on the second syllable of compound roots not analysed in detail (p. 215); rising toneme (and the falling-glide allotone of high tone) effectively confined to stressed root syllables; non-phonemic vowel lengthening only in stressed (root) syllables; Spanish-bilingual speakers drop pitch on final unstressed suffix syllables. Fn. 13 considers and rejects the Weitlaner / Leon & Swadesh hypothesis that stress coincides with high tone for this dialect.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (morphological) word: one strong stress per word on the root-initial syllable, described from both isolated words and connected utterances (phonetic transcriptions of phrases given). Language is tonal (3 tonemes on root syllables, high/low on prefixes); stress statement is explicit and separate from tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Andrews 1949 describes the Otomi of San Pedro Arriba, municipio de Temoaya, Estado de México — the core Temoaya Otomi [ott] = temo1245 (with footnote asides on San Andrés Timilpan). Glottolog also files Lastra's 'otomí de Toluca' (San Andrés Cuexcontitlán; Lastra 1989, 1992; Mijangos 2020) under temo1245; those Toluca sources give tones only and are silent on stress placement. Leon & Swadesh 1949 (saved for context) is about Mezquital Otomi, not this language.

sources.note: Sec. 1.4.1 (pp. 216-217): root-initial juncture is realized as stress on the first syllable of the root; this strong stress occurs nowhere else in the word; prefixes and suffixes unstressed; a light secondary stress sometimes on the second syllable before and after the root syllable; stress and tone (3 tonemes) not conditioned by one another except rising glide limited to stressed (root) syllables; non-phonemic vowel lengthening only in stressed (root) syllables; fn. 13 rejects Weitlaner's and Leon & Swadesh's stress=high-tone reanalysis for Temoaya.

sources.note: About MEZQUITAL Otomi, not Temoaya: reanalyses Sinclair & Pike's three tonemes as a partly free pitch-stress accent (trisyllables and longer with automatic initial accent). Context only; Andrews fn. 13 explicitly rejects this analysis for the Temoaya dialect.
